title: As It Is · 美国生活
zh: VOA 中级文章：美国节日、饮食、城市、历史与日常生活，外加 As It Is 报道。每篇 3～10 分钟，分段中文翻译。
credit: 听力内容来自 VOA Learning English（As It Is、Arts & Culture 等栏目，仅收录 VOA 自己撰写的文章），公共领域，learningenglish.voanews.com

lessons.title: A History of Christmas in America
lessons.zh: 美国圣诞节的历史
lessons.sum: 19 世纪上半叶，圣诞节在美国还不是正式节日，各地过法不同。移民带来了圣诞树、互赠礼物等传统，作家华盛顿·欧文的作品也影响了人们对圣诞节和圣诞老人的想象，圣诞节逐渐成为全国性的节日。

lines.en: From VOA Learning English, I'm Caty Weaver.
lines.zh: 这里是 VOA 慢速英语，我是凯蒂·韦弗。

lines.en: Today, Steve Ember and Shirley Griffith present a special program on Christmas traditions in the United States during the first half of the 19th century.
lines.zh: 今天，史蒂夫·恩伯和雪莉·格里菲斯为您带来一期特别节目，介绍 19 世纪上半叶美国的圣诞传统。

lines.en: During this period, there was no set way of celebrating the day, which was not yet an official holiday. Communities around the country honored the day in different ways. Some observed Christmas as an important Christian religious day honoring the birth of Jesus. Others celebrated the day with parties, music, drinking and eating. And, some communities did not celebrate the day at all.
lines.zh: 那个时期，圣诞节还不是正式节日，也没有固定的过法。全国各地的社区以不同方式纪念这一天。有些人把圣诞节当作纪念耶稣诞生的重要基督教宗教节日；有些人用聚会、音乐、喝酒和吃饭来庆祝；还有一些社区根本不过这个节。

lines.en: But, it was during this period that Americans began to reinvent the holiday. They combined ancient Christmas traditions from different cultures with modern American influences.
lines.zh: 但正是在这一时期，美国人开始重新塑造这个节日。他们把来自不同文化的古老圣诞传统与现代美国的影响结合了起来。

lines.en: Here are Steve Ember and Shirley Griffith.
lines.zh: 下面请史蒂夫·恩伯和雪莉·格里菲斯。

lines.en: In 1819, the popular American writer Washington Irving wrote a series of five essays published in a book called The Sketchbook of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
lines.zh: 1819 年，美国著名作家华盛顿·欧文写了五篇系列随笔，收录在《杰弗里·克雷恩绅士的见闻札记》一书中。

lines.en: The essays describe a wealthy British landowner who invites his farm workers into his home to celebrate Christmas. The landowner recreates a traditional Christmas as it would have been celebrated in the distant past. Irving praised this looking back to ancient traditions. He liked the idea of different levels of society coming together to enjoy a festive and peaceful holiday. Washington Irving seemed to express concern about the lack of such unifying Christmas traditions in modern America.
lines.zh: 这些随笔描写了一位富有的英国地主，他邀请农场工人到家里一起过圣诞节。这位地主重现了遥远过去那种传统的圣诞节。欧文赞美这种回归古老传统的做法。他喜欢社会各阶层聚在一起，共度一个喜庆祥和的节日。华盛顿·欧文似乎担心，现代美国缺少这种凝聚人心的圣诞传统。

lines.en: Penne Restad wrote a book Christmas in America: A History. It shows how Americans began to slowly shape Christmas into a unifying national holiday during the first half of the 19th century. She describes how Christmas had different meanings for Americans who came from different cultural and religious backgrounds. Many immigrants brought Christmas traditions from their own countries.
lines.zh: 彭妮·雷斯塔德写了一本书《美国的圣诞节：一部历史》。书中讲述了 19 世纪上半叶美国人如何慢慢把圣诞节塑造成一个凝聚全国的节日。她描述了圣诞节对来自不同文化和宗教背景的美国人有着不同的意义。许多移民带来了自己国家的圣诞传统。

lines.en: Religion played a big role in how an American might celebrate the holiday. Calvinist Christians banned the celebration of Christmas. But groups such as Episcopalians and Moravians honored the day with religious services and seasonal decorations.
lines.zh: 宗教在美国人怎样过节这件事上起了很大作用。加尔文派基督徒禁止庆祝圣诞节，而圣公会和摩拉维亚教会等团体则用宗教仪式和节日装饰来纪念这一天。

lines.en: By mid-century, Christian groups began to ignore their religious differences over the meaning of Christmas and honored the day in special ways.
lines.zh: 到了 19 世纪中叶，各基督教团体开始不再计较对圣诞节意义的宗教分歧，以各自特别的方式纪念这一天。

lines.en: Christmas became an important time for families to celebrate at home. More and more Christian Americans also began to follow the European traditions of Christmas trees and giving gifts. Christians believed that the tree represented Jesus and was also a sign of new beginnings. German immigrants brought their tradition of putting lights, sweets and toys on the branches of evergreen trees placed in their homes.
lines.zh: 圣诞节成了家人在家团聚庆祝的重要时刻。越来越多的美国基督徒也开始效仿欧洲人摆圣诞树、送礼物的传统。基督徒认为圣诞树代表耶稣，也象征着新的开始。德国移民带来了他们的传统：在家里摆一棵常青树，在树枝上挂灯、糖果和玩具。

lines.en: This tradition of setting up a Christmas tree soon spread to many American homes. So did the practice of giving people presents. As these traditions increased in popularity, the modern trade and business linked to Christmas also grew.
lines.zh: 摆圣诞树的传统很快传遍了许多美国家庭，送礼物的习俗也是如此。随着这些传统越来越流行，与圣诞节相关的现代商业也发展起来了。

lines.en: As Christmas became more popular, some states declared the day a state holiday. Louisiana was the first state to make the move in 1837. By 1860, 14 other states had followed. It was not until 1870 that President Ulysses Grant made Christmas a federal holiday.
lines.zh: 随着圣诞节越来越受欢迎，一些州宣布这一天为州假日。路易斯安那州在 1837 年第一个这样做。到 1860 年，又有 14 个州跟进。直到 1870 年，尤利西斯·格兰特总统才把圣诞节定为联邦假日。

lines.en: Americans already knew old Christmas songs that came from England and other areas of Europe. But many new American Christmas songs started to become popular. For example, in eighteen forty-nine, a religious leader from Massachusetts wrote the words to It Came Upon a Midnight Clear.The song Jingle Bells appeared seven years later. And, a year later, a religious leader in Williamsport, Pennsylvania wrote the song We Three Kings of Orient Are.
lines.zh: 美国人早就熟悉来自英国和欧洲其他地区的古老圣诞歌曲。但很多新的美国圣诞歌曲也开始流行起来。比如 1849 年，马萨诸塞州一位宗教领袖写了《夜半歌声清朗》的歌词。七年后出现了《铃儿响叮当》。再过一年，宾夕法尼亚州威廉斯波特的一位宗教领袖写了《我们是东方三贤士》。

lines.en: And of course, no discussion of Christmas would be complete without talking about of one of the holiday's most famous representations, Santa Claus.
lines.zh: 当然，谈圣诞节不能不谈这个节日最著名的形象之一——圣诞老人。

lines.en: This character is based on the story of Saint Nicholas, a Christian holy person believed to have lived in the third century. Saint Nicholas became known as a protector of children. Different cultures have given him different names. These include Sinterklaas, Kris Kringle and Father Christmas. But for most Americans his most popular name would become Santa Claus.
lines.zh: 这个人物来源于圣尼古拉斯的故事，据信他是生活在公元 3 世纪的一位基督教圣人。圣尼古拉斯被看作儿童的保护者。不同文化给他起了不同的名字，比如辛特克拉斯、克里斯·克林格尔和圣诞老爹。但对大多数美国人来说，他最流行的名字成了“圣诞老人”（Santa Claus）。

lines.en: In the 19th century, many Dutch immigrants living in the United States celebrated the feast of Saint Nicholas on December 6. Saint Nicholas was especially important to New Yorkers because of their history as a Dutch colony. In 1809, Washington Irving published his History of New York. It lists Saint Nicholas as the patron saint of New Yorkers. He describes the saint wearing a low hat, large pants, and smoking a pipe. Does this description sound familiar?
lines.zh: 19 世纪，许多住在美国的荷兰移民在 12 月 6 日庆祝圣尼古拉斯节。由于纽约曾是荷兰殖民地，圣尼古拉斯对纽约人尤其重要。1809 年，华盛顿·欧文出版了《纽约外史》，书中把圣尼古拉斯列为纽约人的守护圣人。他描写的圣人戴着一顶矮帽子，穿着肥大的裤子，抽着烟斗。这个形象听起来是不是很眼熟？

qs.q: When did Christmas become a federal holiday?
qs.why: "It was not until 1870 that President Ulysses Grant made Christmas a federal holiday."

qs.q: Who brought the tradition of decorating evergreen trees?
qs.why: "German immigrants brought their tradition of putting lights, sweets and toys on the branches."

qs.q: Which state first made Christmas a state holiday?
qs.why: "Louisiana was the first state to make the move in 1837."

lessons.title: Thanksgiving: An American Tradition
lessons.zh: 感恩节：美国传统
lessons.sum: 感恩节在每年 11 月的第四个星期四。烤火鸡、填料、南瓜派是餐桌主角；人们长途跋涉回家团聚，年轻人过“朋友感恩节”，还有梅西百货大游行、橄榄球赛和“火鸡跑”。

lines.en: The American holiday of Thanksgiving is celebrated every year on the fourth Thursday in November. The holiday is during autumn -- the main season for harvesting crops. Thanksgiving is an autumn harvest festival like those found in many cultures around the world.
lines.zh: 美国的感恩节在每年 11 月的第四个星期四。这个节日在秋天——收获庄稼的主要季节。感恩节和世界上许多文化中的秋收节一样。

lines.en: On this day, most Americans gather with friends and family. Many take time to think about what they are thankful for, cook up a storm, and eat.
lines.zh: 这一天，大多数美国人和亲朋好友团聚。很多人会花点时间想想自己要感谢什么，然后大做一桌菜，大吃一顿。

lines.en: A lot.
lines.zh: 吃很多。

lines.en: The star of most Thanksgiving dinners is a roasted turkey. Turkeys are large birds native to North America.
lines.zh: 大多数感恩节晚餐的主角是烤火鸡。火鸡是原产于北美的大型鸟类。

lines.en: The turkey is cooked in an oven for many hours, often with a mix of celery, bread, onions and spices inside the bird. This mix becomes stuffing -- another star of the Thanksgiving dinner table.
lines.zh: 火鸡要在烤箱里烤好几个小时，肚子里常常塞着芹菜、面包、洋葱和香料的混合物。这些混合物就成了“填料”——感恩节餐桌上的另一个主角。

lines.en: Anna Matteo here at Learning English says the smell of turkey and stuffing roasting together is the quintessential smell of Thanksgiving. "Quintessential" means the perfect example of something.
lines.zh: VOA 慢速英语的安娜·马泰奥说，火鸡和填料一起烤的香味，是感恩节最典型的味道。“quintessential”的意思是某事物最完美的典型。

lines.en: After the bird is cooked, the stuffing is taken out and served as a side dish.
lines.zh: 火鸡烤好后，把填料取出来，作为配菜上桌。

lines.en: One of many side dishes. Families often make other foods like mashed potatoes, sweet potatoes, cranberry sauce and vegetable casseroles. A casserole is a dish that cooks slowly in an oven.
lines.zh: 这只是众多配菜之一。家家户户常常还会做土豆泥、红薯、蔓越莓酱和蔬菜砂锅。砂锅菜就是在烤箱里慢慢烤的菜。

lines.en: And do not forget about the gravy. This rich sauce is made from the fatty liquid that comes off the turkey as it cooks. People cover their turkey meat, stuffing and mashed potatoes with gravy.
lines.zh: 别忘了肉汁。这种浓郁的酱汁是用火鸡烤的时候流出来的油汁做的。人们会把肉汁浇在火鸡肉、填料和土豆泥上。

lines.en: The meal does not end with the turkey, stuffing, and side dishes, though. For some people, the best part of the meal is dessert.
lines.zh: 不过，这顿饭并不是吃完火鸡、填料和配菜就结束了。对一些人来说，最棒的部分是甜点。

lines.en: The quintessential Thanksgiving dessert is pie. Pumpkin, cherry, apple or pecan pie are all great ways to finish off a Thanksgiving meal...if you are not too full of food by that point!
lines.zh: 最典型的感恩节甜点是派。南瓜派、樱桃派、苹果派或山核桃派都是给感恩节大餐收尾的好选择……如果到那时你还没吃撑的话！

lines.en: Some Americans must travel long distances to be with their families. In fact, the Sunday after Thanksgiving is the busiest travel day of the entire year. This is usually when people return home from family gatherings.
lines.zh: 有些美国人得长途跋涉才能和家人团聚。事实上，感恩节后的那个星期天是全年出行最繁忙的一天，通常这时人们从家庭聚会返回。

lines.en: Not everyone can make the return home each Thanksgiving. So, young people living in cities away from their hometowns sometimes celebrate "Friendsgiving" -- a Thanksgiving meal with their friends instead of their family. They gather at someone's apartment or house and have a "potluck." This is a meal where everyone who is invited brings food to share with others.
lines.zh: 不是每个人每年感恩节都能回家。所以，在离家乡很远的城市生活的年轻人有时会过“朋友感恩节”——和朋友而不是家人一起吃感恩节大餐。他们聚在某人的公寓或房子里，搞一个“百家餐”，也就是每位受邀的人都带一道菜来分享。

lines.en: Thanksgiving is a big day for television, games and other entertainment.
lines.zh: 感恩节也是看电视、比赛和其他娱乐的好日子。

lines.en: One tradition is the television broadcast of Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. It takes place each year in New York City. Workers of the Macy's store on Herald Square organized the first parade in 1924. Many of the workers were immigrants and wanted to hold a big parade like the ones in Europe. So, they dressed in costumes and borrowed some animals from the zoo. They also carried small balloons that floated just overhead.
lines.zh: 一个传统是电视转播梅西百货感恩节大游行。游行每年在纽约市举行。1924 年，先驱广场梅西百货的员工组织了第一次游行。许多员工是移民，想办一场像欧洲那样的大游行。于是他们穿上节日服装，从动物园借来一些动物，还举着在头顶上方飘着的小气球。

lines.en: Many professional American football games are also played on Thanksgiving. Fans of the sport enjoy relaxing and watching a game or two after eating a big Thanksgiving meal.
lines.zh: 感恩节还有许多职业橄榄球比赛。球迷们吃完丰盛的感恩节大餐后，喜欢放松一下，看一两场比赛。

lines.en: Some start Thanksgiving Day early - and in a healthy way. So-called "Turkey Trot" races take place in many towns and cities. These events involve runners dressing up in a Thanksgiving-related costume and running a short distance -- usually five kilometers.
lines.zh: 有些人很早就开始过感恩节——而且方式很健康。许多城镇都有所谓的“火鸡跑”比赛。参加的人穿上和感恩节有关的服装，跑一小段距离，通常是五公里。

lines.en: Many Turkey Trots urge runners to bring canned food to donate to local food banks -- non-profit organizations that give food to poor people in a community.
lines.zh: 许多“火鸡跑”鼓励参赛者带罐头食品，捐给当地的食物银行——给社区穷人提供食物的非营利组织。

lines.en: Certainly, not everyone in America has an easy Thanksgiving. The United States is home to many poor and homeless people. Some cannot afford a Thanksgiving dinner. Others are without friends or families. Many religious and service organizations around the country try to fill these needs. Some provide community dinners at churches and other centers. Some groups also deliver Thanksgiving meals to people too sick or old to leave their homes.
lines.zh: 当然，并不是每个美国人都能轻松过感恩节。美国有很多穷人和无家可归的人。有些人吃不起感恩节晚餐，有些人没有朋友或家人。全国许多宗教和服务组织努力满足这些需求，有的在教堂和其他中心提供社区晚餐，还有一些团体给病得或老得出不了门的人送感恩节餐。

lines.en: The writer O. Henry called Thanksgiving the one holiday that is purely American. It is not linked to a religion or a certain group. Anyone in the United States on the fourth Thursday of November is welcome to celebrate Thanksgiving.
lines.zh: 作家欧·亨利称感恩节是唯一纯粹属于美国的节日。它不与某个宗教或某个群体挂钩。11 月第四个星期四在美国的任何人，都欢迎一起过感恩节。

lines.en: I'm Caty Weaver.
lines.zh: 我是凯蒂·韦弗。

lines.en: And I'm Ashley Thompson.
lines.zh: 我是阿什莉·汤普森。

qs.q: When is Thanksgiving?
qs.why: "celebrated every year on the fourth Thursday in November."

qs.q: What is a "potluck"?
opts: a meal where everyone brings food to share
qs.a: a meal where everyone brings food to share
qs.why: "a meal where everyone who is invited brings food to share."

qs.q: What is the busiest travel day of the year?
qs.why: "the Sunday after Thanksgiving is the busiest travel day of the entire year."

gloss: 百家餐（每人带一道菜的聚餐）

lessons.title: Halloween in America
lessons.zh: 美国的万圣节：服装、糖果和花费
lessons.sum: 10 月 31 日是万圣节。它源于古代不列颠凯尔特人的信仰，如今主要是孩子们的节日：穿上服装挨家挨户喊“不给糖就捣蛋”。美国人每年为万圣节花上百亿美元买服装、糖果和装饰。

lines.en: October 31 is Halloween. But many Americans have been preparing for the holiday for weeks. And businesses are hoping for good profits from Halloween purchases.
lines.zh: 10 月 31 日是万圣节。不过很多美国人几个星期前就开始为这个节日做准备了。商家也希望从万圣节消费中赚上一笔。

lines.en: The National Retail Federation (N.R.F.) is the largest U.S. trade group representing sellers of material goods. It expects total Halloween spending in 2024 to reach about $11.6 billion. That sounds like a healthy amount, but it would be a drop from the year before. The N.R.F. says total Halloween spending in 2023 was a record-setting $12.2 billion.
lines.zh: 全美零售联合会（N.R.F.）是代表商品零售商的美国最大的行业组织。它预计 2024 年万圣节总消费将达到约 116 亿美元。这听起来是个可观的数字，但比前一年有所下降。全美零售联合会说，2023 年万圣节总消费达到创纪录的 122 亿美元。

lines.en: So, you might wonder: What are Americans buying for Halloween and how do they celebrate the holiday?
lines.zh: 你也许会想：美国人为万圣节买什么？又是怎么过这个节的？

lines.en: Halloween traditions in America are linked to Celtic beliefs in ancient Britain. The Celts believed that spirits of the dead would return to their homes on October 31, the day of the autumn feast. Celts would build huge fires to frighten away any evil spirits that might return.
lines.zh: 美国的万圣节传统与古代不列颠凯尔特人的信仰有关。凯尔特人相信，死者的灵魂会在 10 月 31 日——秋季节日那天——回到家里。他们会点起大火，吓跑可能回来的恶灵。

lines.en: People from Scotland and Ireland brought these ideas with them when they came to America. Some believed that spirits played tricks on people on the last night of October.
lines.zh: 苏格兰人和爱尔兰人来到美国时，把这些观念也带了过来。有些人相信，在 10 月的最后一夜，灵魂会捉弄人。

lines.en: In modern America, the holiday mostly belongs to children. After dark, children wear special clothing, called costumes. They often appear as frightening creatures like vampires, ghosts and witches. The children walk around their neighborhoods, knocking on doors of homes. When someone answers a door, the children yell "trick or treat." If the people in the homes do not give them a sweet treat, the children may play a trick on them.
lines.zh: 在现代美国，这个节日主要属于孩子。天黑后，孩子们穿上特别的衣服，叫作“装扮服”。他们常常扮成吸血鬼、鬼魂、女巫这类吓人的形象。孩子们在附近街区走来走去，敲各家的门。有人开门时，孩子们就喊“不给糖就捣蛋！”如果家里的人不给他们糖果，孩子们可能会捉弄他们。

lines.en: Some of the purchases people make for Halloween include candy and costumes. This year, the N.R.F. expects the superhero character Spider-Man to be the most popular children's costume.
lines.zh: 人们为万圣节买的东西包括糖果和装扮服。全美零售联合会预计，今年最受欢迎的儿童装扮是超级英雄角色蜘蛛侠。

lines.en: Children are not the only Americans in costumes on Halloween, however. Adults also dress up in costumes and attend Halloween parties, parades and other events. These celebrations often include costume competitions, with prizes for the most frightening, inventive or humorous costumes.
lines.zh: 不过，万圣节穿装扮服的不只是孩子。成年人也会打扮起来，参加万圣节派对、游行和其他活动。这些庆祝活动常常有装扮比赛，给最吓人、最有创意或最滑稽的装扮发奖。

lines.en: Overall, the N.R.F. reports, total spending on costumes for Halloween 2024 is expected to reach a total of $3.8 billion. It says buyers will spend $3.5 billion on Halloween candy.
lines.zh: 全美零售联合会报告说，总体来看，2024 年万圣节的装扮服消费预计将达到 38 亿美元，万圣节糖果消费 35 亿美元。

lines.en: Americans also enjoy decorating their homes for Halloween.
lines.zh: 美国人也喜欢为万圣节装饰自己的家。

lines.en: People hang fake skeletons, witches, spiders and other scary things around their doors and from trees and bushes. They also cut scary faces into pumpkins and light them to create a strange glow.
lines.zh: 人们在门口、树上和灌木丛上挂假骷髅、女巫、蜘蛛和其他吓人的东西。他们还在南瓜上刻出吓人的脸，在里面点上灯，发出奇异的光。

lines.en: Some people do a little decorating, others do a lot, and still others do none at all. But, the N.R.F. says researchers estimate Americans will spend about $3.8 billion dollars to dress up their houses for Halloween this year.
lines.zh: 有人装饰一点点，有人装饰很多，还有人完全不装饰。不过全美零售联合会说，研究人员估计今年美国人将花约 38 亿美元来装扮房子过万圣节。

lines.en: I'm Caty Weaver.
lines.zh: 我是凯蒂·韦弗。

qs.q: What do children say when someone opens the door?
qs.why: "the children yell 'trick or treat.'"

qs.q: Where do Halloween traditions come from?
qs.why: "linked to Celtic beliefs in ancient Britain."

qs.q: What children's costume was expected to be most popular?
qs.why: "the superhero character Spider-Man"

lessons.title: Independence Day in the US
lessons.zh: 美国独立日
lessons.sum: 美国在 7 月 4 日庆祝独立日。其实大陆会议投票宣布独立是在 7 月 2 日，约翰·亚当斯一直坚持该在那天庆祝。如今各地用烟花、游行、音乐和美食庆祝“美国的生日”。

lines.en: The United States celebrates its Independence Day on July 4.
lines.zh: 美国在 7 月 4 日庆祝独立日。

lines.en: John Adams, who later became America's second president, wrote to his wife in 1776 that the day would be remembered with fireworks and celebrations "from one End of this Continent to the other."
lines.zh: 后来成为美国第二任总统的约翰·亚当斯在 1776 年写信给妻子说，人们将用烟花和庆典纪念这一天，“从这片大陆的一头到另一头”。

lines.en: But the day he was talking about was July 2, 1776, not July 4. July 2 is the day the Continental Congress of the original 13 colonies voted for independence from Britain. Congress did not officially sign the Declaration of Independence, mainly written by Thomas Jefferson, until two days later.
lines.zh: 可他说的那天是 1776 年 7 月 2 日，而不是 7 月 4 日。7 月 2 日是最初 13 个殖民地的大陆会议投票决定脱离英国独立的日子。主要由托马斯·杰斐逊起草的《独立宣言》，直到两天后才被国会正式签署。

lines.en: Pauline Maier was a historian who wrote the 1997 book American Scripture: Making the Declaration of Independence. She wrote that in early July of 1777, members of the Continental Congress nearly forgot that it had been a year since they declared their freedom from the British.
lines.zh: 历史学家波琳·迈尔在 1997 年写了一本书《美国圣经：〈独立宣言〉的诞生》。她写道，1777 年 7 月初，大陆会议的成员们差点忘了他们宣布脱离英国、获得自由已经一年了。

lines.en: They remembered on July 3. It was too late to celebrate on July 2. So, they decided to mark the country's independence with a celebration the following day: July 4.
lines.zh: 他们在 7 月 3 日才想起来。在 7 月 2 日庆祝已经来不及了，所以他们决定第二天——7 月 4 日——举行庆祝活动，纪念国家独立。

lines.en: The Pennsylvania Evening Post of Philadelphia reported, "Yesterday the 4th of July, being the anniversary of the Independence of the United States of America, was celebrated in this city with demonstrations of joy and festivity."
lines.zh: 费城的《宾夕法尼亚晚邮报》报道说：“昨天 7 月 4 日，是美利坚合众国独立周年纪念日，本市以欢乐喜庆的活动庆祝了这一天。”

lines.en: At night, the Post said, "There was a grand exhibition of fireworks…and the city was beautifully illuminated."
lines.zh: 该报说，晚上“有盛大的烟花表演……全城灯火辉煌，十分美丽”。

lines.en: The tradition of celebrating Independence Day started to expand after the War of 1812 against Britain. Such celebrations were mostly held on July 4.
lines.zh: 1812 年对英战争之后，庆祝独立日的传统开始扩大，这些庆祝活动大多在 7 月 4 日举行。

lines.en: John Adams, however, still believed that Americans should celebrate their independence on July 2. Historians say Adams reportedly turned down invitations to take part in July 4 events until the day he died. Adams died on July 4, 1826.
lines.zh: 然而约翰·亚当斯仍然认为美国人应该在 7 月 2 日庆祝独立。历史学家说，据报道亚当斯直到去世都拒绝参加 7 月 4 日的活动。亚当斯于 1826 年 7 月 4 日去世。

lines.en: That same day, Thomas Jefferson also died. The two men and former presidents were friends as well as rivals. They both died on the 50th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence.
lines.zh: 同一天，托马斯·杰斐逊也去世了。这两位前总统既是朋友，也是对手。他们都在《独立宣言》签署 50 周年那天去世。

lines.en: In 1870, the U.S. Congress made July 4th an official holiday.
lines.zh: 1870 年，美国国会把 7 月 4 日定为正式假日。

lines.en: In July 1776, the U.S. was a country of 2.5 million people. It is now a country of 336 million, the U.S. Census reports. These days, Americans celebrate Independence Day with fireworks and other festivities.
lines.zh: 据美国人口普查局报告，1776 年 7 月，美国是一个有 250 万人口的国家，如今已有 3.36 亿人口。现在，美国人用烟花和其他庆祝活动来过独立日。

lines.en: In Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, organizers are holding a 16-day festival of fireworks, music, and food to celebrate "America's birthday in America's birthplace!"
lines.zh: 在宾夕法尼亚州费城，组织者举办了一个为期 16 天的烟花、音乐和美食节，在“美国的诞生地庆祝美国的生日”！

lines.en: But the biggest Fourth of July fireworks show is in New York City. It can be seen in the neighboring states of New Jersey and Connecticut. It is also broadcast nationwide on television.
lines.zh: 但规模最大的 7 月 4 日烟花表演在纽约市。邻近的新泽西州和康涅狄格州都能看到，全国也有电视转播。

lines.en: The small village of Lewes, Delaware celebrates the holiday and its coastal history with the Independence Day Boat Parade.
lines.zh: 特拉华州的小村庄刘易斯用“独立日船只游行”来庆祝节日、纪念它的海滨历史。

lines.en: In Los Angeles, California, movie lovers can choose to celebrate the holiday by watching old Hollywood films from the grassy area of the historic Hollywood Forever cemetery.
lines.zh: 在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶，电影爱好者可以选择在历史悠久的好莱坞永恒公墓的草地上看老好莱坞电影来过节。

lines.en: And far north in Anchorage, Alaska, Independence Day traditions include food, games and late-night fireworks. With 19 hours of daylight this time of year, the fireworks show does not start until midnight.
lines.zh: 而在遥远北方的阿拉斯加州安克雷奇，独立日的传统包括美食、游戏和深夜烟花。每年这个时候那里白天有 19 个小时，所以烟花表演要到午夜才开始。

lines.en: I'm Jill Robbins.
lines.zh: 我是吉尔·罗宾斯。

qs.q: On which day did Congress vote for independence?
qs.why: "July 2 is the day the Continental Congress... voted for independence."

qs.q: What happened on July 4, 1826?
opts: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died.
qs.a: John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died.
qs.why: 两人都在《独立宣言》签署 50 周年那天去世。

qs.q: Why do fireworks in Anchorage start at midnight?
qs.why: "With 19 hours of daylight this time of year."

lessons.title: Cookbooks Show American Culture
lessons.zh: 从食谱看美国文化
lessons.sum: 从 1796 年美国第一本食谱到今天的美食网站，食谱不只教人做菜，还记录了人们一天吃几顿饭、用什么厨具、冰箱何时普及，以及社会和历史的变化。

lines.en: Are you interested in food, United States history, and the English language? If so, American cookbooks provide wide information in all three subjects. The first, published in 1796, started a market that continues in the 21st century with online publications of such works. And, the literature offers more than just recipes.
lines.zh: 你对美食、美国历史和英语感兴趣吗？如果是的话，美国食谱能在这三方面都给你丰富的信息。美国第一本食谱出版于 1796 年，开创了一个延续至今的市场，到 21 世纪还有了在线出版的食谱。而且，这些书提供的不只是菜谱。

lines.en: Megan Elias is the director of food studies at Boston University and the writer of Food on the Page: Cookbooks and American Culture. She says that cookbooks do help teach us how to prepare food. But they provide more than that, too.
lines.zh: 梅根·伊莱亚斯是波士顿大学饮食研究项目主任，著有《纸上的食物：食谱与美国文化》。她说，食谱确实能教我们怎么做饭，但它们提供的远不止这些。

lines.en: "The concept of meals, how many meals a day that people expect to eat? What do they expect to have in those meals?" Elias said.
lines.zh: “关于一日几餐的观念——人们预期一天吃几顿饭？他们期待每顿饭吃些什么？”伊莱亚斯说。

lines.en: They also inform readers about discoveries, equipment and technology related to food making.
lines.zh: 食谱还告诉读者与做饭有关的新发现、新厨具和新技术。

lines.en: Elias said, "What are the objects that are necessary to make the things and what exists? So, are you being asked to do something over an open fire or are you being asked to use an electric stove? Is it something that can be done in the microwave? If you see a lot of recipes for things that are preserved for pickles, you know that you are looking at a time without refrigeration."
lines.zh: 伊莱亚斯说：“做这些菜需要哪些东西？当时有哪些东西？是让你在明火上做，还是用电炉？能不能用微波炉做？如果你看到很多腌菜之类保存食物的菜谱，你就知道那是个没有冰箱的年代。”

lines.en: Amy Bentley is a food historian at New York University. She said that cookbooks from the 1800s were used as lifestyle and household guides. They include food recipes, but they were not central to the books back then.
lines.zh: 艾米·本特利是纽约大学的食物历史学家。她说，19 世纪的食谱是生活和持家指南。书里有菜谱，但在当时，菜谱并不是这些书的核心。

lines.en: "So, there's some recipes for food, but it could be recipes for a cleaning solvent or what to do when your child has been poisoned, how to clean, how to get stains out," Bentley said.
lines.zh: “所以书里有一些做菜的方子，但也可能有清洁溶剂的配方，或者孩子中毒了怎么办，怎么打扫，怎么去污渍。”本特利说。

lines.en: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons is the first cookbook published in the United States. Simmons wrote that her goal with the book was to improve the new generation of women in the U.S.
lines.zh: 阿米莉亚·西蒙斯的《美国烹饪》是在美国出版的第一本食谱。西蒙斯写道，她写这本书的目的是提升美国新一代女性。

lines.en: Megan Elias says that after the Civil War, cookbooks became more diverse. Writers started exploring local foods and customs in their work.
lines.zh: 梅根·伊莱亚斯说，南北战争之后，食谱变得更加多样。作者们开始在书中探索各地的食物和习俗。

lines.en: Elias said that Southern cookbooks tried to offer "… a beautiful version of the old South that will kind of heal over the wounds of the Civil War rather than dealing with the problems that caused the Civil War to begin with."
lines.zh: 伊莱亚斯说，南方的食谱试图呈现“……一个美好的旧南方形象，来抚平南北战争的创伤，而不是去面对引发南北战争的那些问题”。

lines.en: Some communities would put together a group cookbook to raise money. These cookbooks provide a look into what the American middle class was eating throughout the years. Such works serve as a record of the traditions and interests of different neighborhoods and groups.
lines.zh: 有些社区会合编一本食谱来筹款。这些食谱让人看到多年来美国中产阶级在吃什么，记录了不同街区和群体的传统与兴趣。

lines.en: Throughout the years cookbooks have signified humanity's growth in knowledge, trends and innovations. During the last part of the 19th century, for example, many recipes were informed by the dangers of food containing bacteria. Then, in the 1930s, refrigerators became common objects in American homes. The threat of bacterial infection from food dropped, and very soon, cooks adapted to the new conditions. New recipes and new cookbooks resulted.
lines.zh: 多年来，食谱标志着人类在知识、潮流和创新上的进步。比如 19 世纪后期，许多菜谱都考虑到食物中细菌的危险。后来到了 20 世纪 30 年代，冰箱在美国家庭中普及，食物引起细菌感染的威胁下降了，厨师们很快适应了新条件，新菜谱和新食谱随之出现。

lines.en: But cookbooks are not complete reflections of American life. Elias said publishing companies mostly control cookbook content. And, their main goal is to make money from book sales.
lines.zh: 不过，食谱并不能完整地反映美国生活。伊莱亚斯说，食谱的内容主要由出版公司控制，而它们的主要目标是靠卖书赚钱。

lines.en: "The publishing world doesn't necessarily have the goal of representing the truth of Americans who made it. It tends to be upper middle class, white, Northeastern."
lines.zh: “出版界的目标不一定是展现创造这些菜的美国人的真实面貌。它往往偏向中上阶层、白人、东北部。”

lines.en: In the 21st century, with the growth of social media and food websites, publishing companies have less control. These new ways to share recipes have led to more open discussions about food and cooking. This gives the public more choices and power.
lines.zh: 到了 21 世纪，随着社交媒体和美食网站的发展，出版公司的控制力变小了。这些分享菜谱的新方式让人们对食物和烹饪的讨论更加开放，给了公众更多选择和话语权。

lines.en: Elias praised the new discussions around food.
lines.zh: 伊莱亚斯称赞了这些围绕食物的新讨论。

lines.en: "If you look at the comments on food blogs and on any kind of recipe site, you really get to see what people are cooking, and what they think of how they're cooking, and how they think of themselves as experts."
lines.zh: “如果你看看美食博客和各种菜谱网站上的评论，就能真正看到人们在做什么菜，他们怎么看待自己的做法，以及他们如何把自己看作行家。”

lines.en: Physical cookbooks are still highly desirable as well, Bentley says. "They're very good to give as gifts. They're very, very popular because they're sort of neutral. And everyone loves a cookbook, especially with beautiful pages," she said.
lines.zh: 本特利说，纸质食谱仍然很受欢迎。“它们非常适合当礼物。它们很受欢迎，因为它们有点‘中性’，不会出错。人人都喜欢食谱，尤其是书页漂亮的那种。”她说。

qs.q: When was the first American cookbook published?
qs.why: "The first, published in 1796..."

qs.q: What do recipes for pickles tell you?
opts: It was a time without refrigeration.
qs.a: It was a time without refrigeration.
qs.why: "you know that you are looking at a time without refrigeration."

qs.q: Why are cookbooks good gifts, says Bentley?
opts: They are neutral and everyone loves them.
qs.a: They are neutral and everyone loves them.
qs.why: "because they're sort of neutral. And everyone loves a cookbook."

lessons.title: Louisiana's Creole Culture Extends Far and Wide
lessons.zh: 路易斯安那的克里奥尔文化
lessons.sum: 在路易斯安那州，克里奥尔文化无处不在：柴迪科音乐、秋葵浓汤、红豆饭、狂欢节游行和独特的建筑。“克里奥尔”一词的含义因地因人而异，它与西非和加勒比文化有着深厚的联系。

lines.en: Language experts estimate as many as 10,000 people still speak the French-based language Louisiana Creole.
lines.zh: 语言专家估计，仍有多达一万人在说以法语为基础的路易斯安那克里奥尔语。

lines.en: In addition, many others in New Orleans and across the southern U.S. state consider themselves part of the culture that draws tens of thousands of people to events. The celebrations include autumn's Festival Acadiens et Creoles, summer's Creole Tomato Festival, and spring's Tremé Creole Gumbo & Congo Square Rhythms Festival.
lines.zh: 此外，在新奥尔良和整个路易斯安那州，还有许多人认为自己属于这种文化。相关活动吸引了数以万计的人，包括秋天的阿卡迪亚与克里奥尔节、夏天的克里奥尔番茄节，以及春天的特雷梅克里奥尔秋葵浓汤与刚果广场节奏节。

lines.en: But for locals and visitors alike, everyday evidence shows how strong Creole culture is in Louisiana. The state's performance spaces and airwaves are often filled with the driving, rhythmic sound of zydeco and other Creole and Cajun music. Louisiana's restaurants offer dishes with rich, complex flavors including gumbo, hot sausage, red beans and rice, and shrimp étouffée.
lines.zh: 但无论对当地人还是游客来说，日常生活中处处可见克里奥尔文化在路易斯安那有多么强大。州里的演出场所和电台经常充满柴迪科音乐以及其他克里奥尔和卡津音乐那强劲而富有节奏的声音。路易斯安那的餐馆供应味道浓郁丰富的菜肴，包括秋葵浓汤、辣香肠、红豆饭和炖虾。

lines.en: "To celebrate Creole culture is to wake up and live in New Orleans," said Christina Bragg. She is a member of the Mahogany Blue Babydolls, a parade group for Black and mixed-race women.
lines.zh: “庆祝克里奥尔文化，就是在新奥尔良醒来、生活。”克里斯蒂娜·布拉格说。她是“桃花心木蓝娃娃”的成员，这是一个由黑人和混血女性组成的游行团体。

lines.en: "Celebrating Creole is celebrating our day-to-day lives. The food we eat. The music we dance to. The way we gather with friends to parade during Mardi Gras," she said. "Every day I open my eyes and breathe, it's a celebration of Creole culture, because that's who I am."
lines.zh: “庆祝克里奥尔，就是庆祝我们的日常生活：我们吃的食物，我们跳舞的音乐，我们在狂欢节和朋友聚在一起游行的方式，”她说，“我每天睁开眼睛、呼吸，都是在庆祝克里奥尔文化，因为那就是我。”

lines.en: So, what is Creole?
lines.zh: 那么，克里奥尔到底是什么？

lines.en: "It's food, it's music, it's architecture, it's style and it's traditions," Mona Lisa Saloy told VOA. "There are millions of Creole people in countries across the world…we are all so much more alike than we are different. We create beautiful cultures everywhere we go, and I think that's evident here in Louisiana."
lines.zh: “它是食物，是音乐，是建筑，是风格，也是传统，”莫娜·丽莎·萨洛伊对 VOA 说，“世界各国有数百万克里奥尔人……我们彼此相同之处远多于不同之处。我们走到哪里都创造出美丽的文化，我想在路易斯安那这一点很明显。”

lines.en: Saloy is the writer of the poetry collection Black Creole Chronicles and served as Louisiana's poet laureate from 2021 to 2023. She said Creole cultures all over the world have similarities to Louisiana's.
lines.zh: 萨洛伊著有诗集《黑人克里奥尔编年史》，2021 年至 2023 年担任路易斯安那州桂冠诗人。她说，世界各地的克里奥尔文化都和路易斯安那的有相似之处。

lines.en: "Architectural styles common in New Orleans like the Creole Cottage or the Shotgun home can be found in other places with Creoles, such as in other parts of the American South and the Caribbean," she said. "Much of our music derives from the rhythms of Africa and the Caribbean, as does much of our food — elements of gumbo such as the long rice and okra, for example, or the prevalence of beans."
lines.zh: “新奥尔良常见的建筑风格，比如克里奥尔小屋或‘猎枪屋’，在美国南方其他地区和加勒比海等其他有克里奥尔人的地方也能找到，”她说，“我们的很多音乐源自非洲和加勒比的节奏，我们的很多食物也是如此——比如秋葵浓汤里的长粒米和秋葵，或者豆类的普遍使用。”

lines.en: How the word "Creole" is defined changes from place to place and person to person.
lines.zh: “克里奥尔”这个词怎么定义，因地而异，也因人而异。

lines.en: The word "Creole" is believed to have come from the Portuguese word crioulo, which developed from the Latin word for "to create." Some say it was used in the European slave trade to describe a slave born in the New World and not in Africa. The word took on different meanings in different places. Creole in much of Africa and part of the Caribbean, for example, came to mean people of mixed ethnic or racial backgrounds.
lines.zh: 人们认为“克里奥尔”一词来自葡萄牙语 crioulo，而它又源于拉丁语中表示“创造”的词。有人说，在欧洲的奴隶贸易中，这个词用来指在新大陆而不是在非洲出生的奴隶。这个词在不同地方有了不同的含义。比如，在非洲大部分地区和加勒比部分地区，克里奥尔指的是不同族裔或种族背景混血的人。

lines.en: In Louisiana, the definition has changed over the years.
lines.zh: 在路易斯安那，它的定义多年来也在变化。

lines.en: "Here, the definition kind of depends on who you ask," said Vance Vaucresson. He is a New Orleans-based Creole and owner of a local restaurant, the Vaucresson Sausage Company.
lines.zh: “在这里，定义多少取决于你问谁。”万斯·沃克雷森说。他是新奥尔良的克里奥尔人，经营着一家当地餐馆——沃克雷森香肠公司。

lines.en: "I prefer an inclusive definition," he said. "By that definition, anyone born in Louisiana could be Creole. During our colonial era, it was meant to differentiate people born in the Americas — usually of French, Spanish or African descent — from those born in Europe or Africa."
lines.zh: “我更喜欢包容的定义，”他说，“按照这个定义，任何在路易斯安那出生的人都可以是克里奥尔人。在我们的殖民时代，这个词是用来区分在美洲出生的人——通常是法国、西班牙或非洲后裔——和在欧洲或非洲出生的人。”

lines.en: Describing his definition, Vaucresson added: "…it doesn't matter. If you're born here and embrace the culture, you can be Creole."
lines.zh: 沃克雷森在描述他的定义时补充说：“……其实无所谓。如果你在这里出生，并且拥抱这种文化，你就可以是克里奥尔人。”

lines.en: In Louisiana of the 1700s and 1800s, the more inclusive definition was possibly the most accepted. White people with European ancestry were just as likely to call themselves Creole as mixed-race people of African ancestry.
lines.zh: 在 18 和 19 世纪的路易斯安那，更包容的定义可能是最被接受的。有欧洲血统的白人和有非洲血统的混血人一样，都可能称自己为克里奥尔人。

lines.en: White Creoles claimed the term because it set them apart from settlers who were coming from Northern states after The Louisiana Purchase from France in 1803. Mixed-race Creoles, too, claimed the term because it differentiated them from enslaved people.
lines.zh: 白人克里奥尔人使用这个称呼，是因为它能把他们和 1803 年美国从法国手中购买路易斯安那之后从北方各州迁来的移民区分开。混血的克里奥尔人也使用这个称呼，因为它能把他们和被奴役的人区分开。

lines.en: Don Vappie is a Creole jazz musician in New Orleans. He described the idea of Creole before the Civil war as organized into three levels. "It was more of a three-tier racial hierarchy here, instead of the two-tiered Black-or-white experienced elsewhere in the U.S," he said.
lines.zh: 唐·瓦皮是新奥尔良的一位克里奥尔爵士乐手。他说，南北战争之前的克里奥尔观念分为三个等级。“这里更像是一个三层的种族等级制度，而不是美国其他地方那种非黑即白的两层制度。”他说。

lines.en: After the American Civil War, however, many of these differences in New Orleans disappeared.
lines.zh: 然而，南北战争之后，新奥尔良的许多这类区别都消失了。

lines.en: "Creole or not, white people had more in common with white people and Black people had more in common with Black people," Vappie told VOA.
lines.zh: “不管是不是克里奥尔人，白人和白人的共同点更多，黑人和黑人的共同点更多。”瓦皮对 VOA 说。

lines.en: Saloy believes Creole is firmly connected to African culture and should stay that way.
lines.zh: 萨洛伊认为，克里奥尔与非洲文化紧密相连，也应该保持这种联系。

lines.en: "The ingredients in our food, the rhythm in our music and dance, the details in our architecture — it's all connected to West African culture," she said, "That's our heritage."
lines.zh: “我们食物的原料、音乐和舞蹈的节奏、建筑的细节——都和西非文化相连，”她说，“那是我们的传统。”

lines.en: I'm Caty Weaver. And I'm Faith Pirlo.
lines.zh: 我是凯蒂·韦弗。我是费丝·皮尔洛。

qs.q: About how many people still speak Louisiana Creole?
qs.why: "as many as 10,000 people still speak the French-based language Louisiana Creole."

qs.q: Which is a Creole dish?
qs.why: "gumbo, hot sausage, red beans and rice, and shrimp étouffée."

qs.q: Where does the word "Creole" probably come from?
qs.why: "believed to have come from the Portuguese word crioulo."

lessons.title: What White House Gardens Say about America
lessons.zh: 白宫花园里的美国
lessons.sum: 早期总统不想要欧洲君主那样的宫廷花园，杰斐逊还把白宫庭院缩小。后来的总统和第一夫人各有改动：肯尼迪改建玫瑰园，米歇尔·奥巴马开辟了菜园。白宫花园如今每年春秋两季对公众开放。

lines.en: The earliest presidents who lived in the White House did not want the large outdoor areas that the monarchs of Europe might enjoy.
lines.zh: 最早住在白宫的几位总统，并不想要欧洲君主可能享受的那种大片户外园地。

lines.en: Marta McDowell is writer of All the Presidents' Gardens. She said, "You can understand that, given our democratic form of government." But she said she thinks that a visit to the home of the British royal family, Buckingham Palace, caused President John Kennedy to expand the White House gardens.
lines.zh: 玛尔塔·麦克道尔是《总统们的花园》一书的作者。她说：“考虑到我们民主的政府形式，这是可以理解的。”不过她认为，是一次对英国王室住所白金汉宫的访问，促使约翰·肯尼迪总统扩建了白宫花园。

lines.en: From the start, presidents and their families influenced the 7.2 hectares of open space in the front and back of the White House differently. Their choices often showed their values and traditions of their day.
lines.zh: 从一开始，历任总统和他们的家人就以不同方式影响着白宫前后这 7.2 公顷的空地。他们的选择往往体现出那个时代的价值观和传统。

lines.en: McDowell said that the White House is "really their home" while they are in office. She added that as long as they work with the historic plan of the gardens the National Park Service tries to meet the desires of the administration. The National Park Service oversees the gardens.
lines.zh: 麦克道尔说，总统在任期间，白宫“真的是他们的家”。她补充说，只要遵循花园的历史规划，国家公园管理局就会尽量满足本届政府的愿望。白宫花园由国家公园管理局负责管理。

lines.en: John Quincy Adams, America's sixth president, worked in the garden. Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th president, took down glass structures called greenhouses that were first built by James Buchanan, the 15th president, in the 1850s.
lines.zh: 美国第六任总统约翰·昆西·亚当斯曾在花园里劳作。第 26 任总统西奥多·罗斯福拆掉了 19 世纪 50 年代第 15 任总统詹姆斯·布坎南最先建造的玻璃温室。

lines.en: John Kennedy, the 35th president, redesigned one garden called the Rose Garden in the 1960s. First lady Michelle Obama, wife of the 44th president, built a food garden using plants and seeds from the home of Thomas Jefferson, the third president. Today, the garden has more than 50 kinds of vegetables.
lines.zh: 第 35 任总统约翰·肯尼迪在 20 世纪 60 年代重新设计了一个叫“玫瑰园”的花园。第 44 任总统的夫人米歇尔·奥巴马用来自第三任总统托马斯·杰斐逊故居的植物和种子开辟了一个菜园。如今，这个菜园里种着 50 多种蔬菜。

lines.en: Pierre L'Enfant was the city planner and architect for America's first president, George Washington. At first, he planned for a 30-hectare presidential garden. However, as a believer in small government, Jefferson reduced the White House grounds to just 2 hectares. The gardens were expanded to the current 7.2 hectares
lines.zh: 皮埃尔·朗方是美国首任总统乔治·华盛顿的城市规划师和建筑师。起初，他规划了一个 30 公顷的总统花园。可是，杰斐逊信奉小政府，把白宫庭院缩小到只有 2 公顷。后来花园扩大到现在的 7.2 公顷。

lines.en: Jefferson, like many Americans who had just freed themselves from a British monarch, was concerned about creating a new king.
lines.zh: 杰斐逊和许多刚刚摆脱英国君主统治的美国人一样，担心会造出一个新的国王。

lines.en: "Avoid palaces and gardens of palaces," William Thornton, a Washington city representative warned. "If you build a palace with gardens, I will find you a king."
lines.zh: “要避免宫殿和宫殿的花园，”华盛顿市的代表威廉·桑顿警告说，“如果你建了一座带花园的宫殿，我就能给你找出一个国王来。”

lines.en: Over time, several different plants and flowers were planted at the White House. They include roses which have been around since at least Jefferson's time. They also include peonies, wanted by first lady first lady Nancy Reagan of the 40th president, and Texas bluebells, asked for by first lady Laura Bush of the 43rd president.
lines.zh: 随着时间推移，白宫种下了多种花草。其中有至少从杰斐逊时代就有的玫瑰，有第 40 任总统夫人南希·里根想要的牡丹，还有第 43 任总统夫人劳拉·布什要求种的德克萨斯蓝铃花。

lines.en: Oak and elm trees have also been on the White House grounds almost since the beginning. One tree, a chestnut oak southeast of the White House, might be the oldest tree on the grounds. The White House says it has been around since 1800.
lines.zh: 橡树和榆树几乎从一开始就长在白宫的庭院里。白宫东南边的一棵栗栎可能是院子里最老的树。白宫说它从 1800 年就在那里了。

lines.en: McDowell says the White House gardens represent gardening tradition over time. First it followed designs in Europe, and then it was shaped by local traditions, the area, and the climate.
lines.zh: 麦克道尔说，白宫花园代表了园艺传统的演变：起初效仿欧洲的设计，后来又受到本地传统、地域和气候的影响。

lines.en: But she said, "It's not that they are always the leader. In fact, sometimes they're following."
lines.zh: 不过她说：“它们并不总是引领潮流。事实上，有时候它们是在跟随。”

lines.en: The White house grounds were open to the public up until 1923. That was when Calvin Coolidge, the 30th president, permanently closed them to unapproved visitors.
lines.zh: 直到 1923 年，白宫庭院一直对公众开放。那一年，第 30 任总统卡尔文·柯立芝永久禁止未经批准的访客进入。

lines.en: These days, the White House Garden planned visits for the public are usually available for the public twice a year, one weekend in the spring and again in autumn.
lines.zh: 如今，白宫花园通常每年对公众开放两次参观，春天一个周末，秋天一个周末。

lines.en: McDowell said, "They are full of tradition. They're full of beauty."
lines.zh: 麦克道尔说：“它们充满了传统，充满了美。”

lines.en: I'm Gregory Stachel.
lines.zh: 我是格雷戈里·斯塔切尔。

qs.q: Why did early presidents not want big gardens?
opts: They did not want to look like European kings.
qs.a: They did not want to look like European kings.
qs.why: "concerned about creating a new king."

qs.q: What did Michelle Obama build?
qs.why: "built a food garden using plants and seeds from the home of Thomas Jefferson."

qs.q: How often can the public visit the gardens today?
qs.why: "one weekend in the spring and again in autumn."

lessons.title: The Story of Santa Claus
lessons.zh: 圣诞老人的故事
lessons.sum: 圣诞老人坐着驯鹿拉的雪橇从北极飞来，从烟囱钻进屋里往长袜里塞礼物。这个形象来自摩尔的诗《圣尼古拉斯来访》和画家托马斯·纳斯特的画，而他的原型是 4 世纪乐善好施的圣尼古拉斯。

lines.en: Santa Claus is someone who will remain in the hearts of children forever. He is the make-believe person who brings toys and other gifts to children at Christmas. To grown-ups, he is a special symbol of good will and selfless giving.
lines.zh: 圣诞老人会永远留在孩子们心里。他是那个在圣诞节给孩子们带来玩具和礼物的虚构人物。对大人来说，他是善意和无私奉献的特别象征。

lines.en: Santa Claus also has some other names, like Saint Nicholas, Kris Kringle and Pelznickel.
lines.zh: 圣诞老人还有别的名字，比如圣尼古拉斯、克里斯·克林格尔和佩尔茨尼克尔。

lines.en: The Santa Claus we talk about in the United States flies from his home at the North Pole on Christmas Eve to bring toys and gifts to children. The happy, white-bearded man is dressed in red. He usually flies on a sleigh led by his reindeer. Santa enters each home through the chimney and fills children's stockings with toys and gifts.
lines.zh: 在美国，我们说的圣诞老人会在平安夜从北极的家里飞出来，给孩子们送玩具和礼物。这位快乐的白胡子老人穿着一身红衣服，通常坐着驯鹿拉的雪橇飞行。他从烟囱钻进每户人家，往孩子们的长袜里塞满玩具和礼物。

lines.en: This modern image of Santa Claus largely comes from Clement Clark Moore's famous poem, A Visit from St. Nicholas.
lines.zh: 圣诞老人的这种现代形象，很大程度上来自克莱门特·克拉克·摩尔的名诗《圣尼古拉斯来访》。

lines.en: 'Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse; The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that St. Nicholas soon would be there;…
lines.zh: 那是圣诞前夜，整个屋子里，没有一点动静，连老鼠也不出声；长袜小心地挂在烟囱旁，盼着圣尼古拉斯很快就到访；……

lines.en: He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying his finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose;
lines.zh: 他一言不发，径直干起活来，把所有长袜都塞满；然后猛一转身，把手指放在鼻子旁边，点一点头，就顺着烟囱上去了；

lines.en: Santa Claus is believed to have come from the story of St. Nicholas. He was a 4th-century clergy in the Mediterranean port city of Myra, part of modern-day Turkey. It is said that St. Nicholas gave away all his wealth to help the poor and the sick. History.com says St. Nicholas became known as the protector of children and sailors. It adds that he was the most popular saint in Europe.
lines.zh: 人们认为圣诞老人来源于圣尼古拉斯的故事。他是 4 世纪地中海港口城市米拉的一位神职人员，米拉在今天的土耳其境内。据说圣尼古拉斯把全部财产都拿出来帮助穷人和病人。History.com 网站说，圣尼古拉斯被视为儿童和水手的保护者，还说他是欧洲最受欢迎的圣人。

lines.en: In the 18th century, Dutch immigrants brought the story of Saint Nikolaas and the tradition of gift-giving to New York City. The Dutch said his name very quickly. It sounded like "Sinterklaas." When English speakers said this word, it sounded like Santa Claus.
lines.zh: 18 世纪，荷兰移民把圣尼古拉斯的故事和送礼物的传统带到了纽约市。荷兰人说他的名字说得很快，听起来像“辛特克拉斯”（Sinterklaas）。英语使用者说这个词时，听起来就像“圣诞老人”（Santa Claus）。

lines.en: German immigrants working as farmers in the American state of Pennsylvania also knew of Saint Nikolaas. But they called him Pelznickel. This word came from "pelz," meaning fur in German, and "nickel" for Nicholas. Saint Nikolaasor became a man dressed in fur who came once a year with gifts for good children.
lines.zh: 在美国宾夕法尼亚州务农的德国移民也知道圣尼古拉斯，不过他们管他叫“佩尔茨尼克尔”。这个词来自德语里表示“毛皮”的 pelz 和代表尼古拉斯的 nickel。圣尼古拉斯变成了一个穿着毛皮、每年来一次给好孩子送礼物的人。

lines.en: Pelznickel became part of a celebration honoring the Christkindl, as the Germans called the child of Christ. After some time, Christkindl became "Kris Kringle." That is another name you will hear for Santa Claus.
lines.zh: 佩尔茨尼克尔成了纪念“基督圣婴”（德国人叫 Christkindl）的庆祝活动的一部分。过了一段时间，Christkindl 变成了“克里斯·克林格尔”，这是你会听到的圣诞老人的另一个名字。

lines.en: A Santa-liked figure is known as Father Christmas in Britain and Père Noël in France. In Scandinavia, an elf named Jultomten was thought to deliver gifts in a sleigh drawn by goats. In Italy, a woman called La Befana rides a broomstick down the chimneys of homes to bring toys for lucky children.
lines.zh: 类似圣诞老人的人物在英国叫“圣诞老爹”，在法国叫“诺埃尔老爹”。在斯堪的纳维亚，人们认为一个叫尤尔托姆滕的小精灵坐着山羊拉的雪橇送礼物。在意大利，一位叫贝法娜的女人骑着扫帚从烟囱下来，给幸运的孩子们送玩具。

lines.en: The image of Santa Claus as we now see him came from Thomas Nast. He was an American painter born in Bavaria, Germany.
lines.zh: 我们现在看到的圣诞老人形象来自托马斯·纳斯特。他是一位出生在德国巴伐利亚的美国画家。

lines.en: Nast remembered that, when he was a little boy, a kind old man would give toys and cakes to the children on Christmas. So, when Nast painted Santa Claus, he looked like the old man from his childhood.
lines.zh: 纳斯特记得，他小时候，每到圣诞节，有个和善的老人会给孩子们玩具和蛋糕。所以纳斯特画圣诞老人时，画得就像他童年时的那位老人。

lines.en: Nast painted Santa as a short, fat, jolly old man with a long beard. He wore a red suit with white fur. He also gave Santa a North Pole workshop, elves, and a wife, Mrs. Claus. Through the years, Nast's painting has remained the most popular picture of Santa Claus.
lines.zh: 纳斯特把圣诞老人画成一个矮胖、快活、留着长胡子的老人，穿着一身镶白毛边的红衣服。他还给圣诞老人画了北极的工作坊、小精灵，以及一位妻子——圣诞老太太。多年来，纳斯特的画一直是最受欢迎的圣诞老人形象。

lines.en: American children write letters to Santa hoping to be on his "nice list" for Christmas gifts. On Christmas Eve, they leave cookies and milk for Santa and carrots for his reindeer: Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donner, Blitzen and "the most famous reindeer of all," Rudolph.
lines.zh: 美国孩子给圣诞老人写信，希望进入他的圣诞礼物“好孩子名单”。平安夜，他们会给圣诞老人留下饼干和牛奶，给他的驯鹿留下胡萝卜。驯鹿的名字是：冲冲、舞舞、跳跳、狐狐、彗星、丘比特、雷神、闪电，还有“最有名的驯鹿”鲁道夫。

lines.en: I'm Ashley Thompson.
lines.zh: 我是阿什莉·汤普森。

qs.q: How does Santa enter each home?
qs.why: "Santa enters each home through the chimney."

qs.q: Who painted the modern image of Santa?
qs.why: "The image of Santa Claus as we now see him came from Thomas Nast."

qs.q: What do children leave for Santa's reindeer?
qs.why: "carrots for his reindeer"

lessons.title: Boston Common: America's First Public Park
lessons.zh: 波士顿公园：美国第一座公共公园
lessons.sum: 近 400 年前，波士顿殖民者集资买下一块农场作为公共用地，这就是美国最古老的公园。过去人们在这里放牛，如今每年有 700 万游客。公园还计划设立纪念当地原住民马萨诸塞部落的作品。

lines.en: Almost 400 years ago, America's early European colonists voted to tax each household in Boston about $70 in today's money. The money was used to buy a local farm. The plan was to use it as a common area for the public.
lines.zh: 近 400 年前，美国早期的欧洲殖民者投票决定，向波士顿每户人家征收相当于今天约 70 美元的税，用这笔钱买下当地一座农场，作为公众共用的地方。

lines.en: That is how Boston Common, in the state of Massachusetts, became America's first public park.
lines.zh: 马萨诸塞州的波士顿公园（Boston Common）就这样成了美国第一座公共公园。

lines.en: Liz Vizza is president of the Friends of the Public Garden, an organization that supports Boston Common. She noted that Bostonians did not have backyards – private outdoor spaces behind their homes. Boston Common, she said, became "their front yard and backyard and common ground. It was a place that everybody owned."
lines.zh: 莉兹·维扎是“公共花园之友”的主席，这个组织为波士顿公园提供支持。她指出，当时的波士顿人没有后院——也就是房子后面的私人户外空间。她说，波士顿公园成了“他们的前院、后院和公共场地。那是一个人人都拥有的地方”。

lines.en: On any given day, colonists walking though Boston Common would see soldiers setting up camp or their neighbors taking walks. They may also have seen public punishments. Presidents George Washington and John Adams also visited the park.
lines.zh: 在任何一天，穿过波士顿公园的殖民者都可能看到士兵在扎营，或者邻居在散步，也可能看到公开的刑罚。乔治·华盛顿和约翰·亚当斯两位总统也曾到访这座公园。

lines.en: Visitors would have seen cows, because everyone had the right to keep one cow per household in the area.
lines.zh: 游客还会看到牛，因为每户人家都有权在这里养一头牛。

lines.en: Today, visitors will find dogs instead of cows in the 20-hectare park. The cows became outlawed in 1830 as Boston Common became more of a place for recreation.
lines.zh: 如今，在这座 20 公顷的公园里，游客看到的是狗而不是牛。1830 年，随着波士顿公园越来越成为休闲娱乐的场所，牛被禁止进入了。

lines.en: Friends of the Public Garden estimates that Boston Common sees 7 million visitors each year.
lines.zh: 据“公共花园之友”估计，波士顿公园每年有 700 万游客。

lines.en: "Boston Common is a central stage of civic life in Boston and it's been that center stage of civic life for hundreds of years, ever since it began as a park in 1634," Vizza said. "America's oldest park is a place where we come to celebrate, we come to protest, we come to find a place alone," she added.
lines.zh: “波士顿公园是波士顿市民生活的中心舞台，自 1634 年作为公园开始以来，几百年来一直如此，”维扎说，“在美国最古老的公园里，我们来庆祝，我们来抗议，我们也来寻找一个独处的地方。”她补充说。

lines.en: Boston Common is home to several large pieces of art. They include "The Embrace," a sculpture that shows civil rights leader Martin Luther King, Jr. holding his wife, Coretta Scott King. The Brewer Fountain was the park's first public piece of art. It won the top award at the 1855 World's Fair in Paris, France.
lines.zh: 波士顿公园里有几件大型艺术品，其中包括雕塑《拥抱》，表现的是民权领袖马丁·路德·金拥抱妻子科雷塔·斯科特·金。布鲁尔喷泉是公园的第一件公共艺术品，它在 1855 年法国巴黎世界博览会上获得了最高奖。

lines.en: The pieces of art found on the Common may soon change to include a wider selection of subjects.
lines.zh: 公园里的艺术品可能很快会改变，纳入更多元的主题。

lines.en: Vizza said, "We want people to look at it with new eyes and just have a deeper understanding and respect and awareness of the history."
lines.zh: 维扎说：“我们希望人们用新的眼光看待它，对这段历史有更深的理解、尊重和认识。”

lines.en: That history includes the native Massachusett tribe, the first people to live where the Common is now. The state of Massachusetts is named after the Massachusett people.
lines.zh: 这段历史包括原住民马萨诸塞部落，他们是最早住在今天波士顿公园这片土地上的人。马萨诸塞州就是以马萨诸塞人命名的。

lines.en: Vizza said, "People have lived on this land for 12,000 years. So, we do want to think about colonial America because that's a fascinating story for us. But what's an even more fascinating story is to peel those layers open to think about the Native Americans living here."
lines.zh: 维扎说：“人们已经在这片土地上生活了 12000 年。所以，我们确实想讲殖民时期的美国，因为那对我们来说是个迷人的故事。但更迷人的故事是把这些层次一层层剥开，去想想生活在这里的美洲原住民。”

lines.en: Vizza's team is working with tribal members to develop a piece to recognize the Massachusett tribe. They hope to have something in place by 2026, when America will celebrate its 250th birthday.
lines.zh: 维扎的团队正在和部落成员合作，制作一件纪念马萨诸塞部落的作品。他们希望在 2026 年美国庆祝建国 250 周年时落成。

lines.en: I'm Ashley Thompson.
lines.zh: 我是阿什莉·汤普森。

qs.q: What was Boston Common before it became a park?
qs.why: "The money was used to buy a local farm."

qs.q: What animals were once kept on Boston Common?
qs.why: "everyone had the right to keep one cow per household."

qs.q: How many people visit each year?
qs.why: "Boston Common sees 7 million visitors each year."

lessons.title: How Did Thanksgiving 'Turkey' Get Its Name?
lessons.zh: 火鸡为什么叫“土耳其”？
lessons.sum: 英语里火鸡（turkey）和土耳其（Turkey）同名，其实源于一个误会：欧洲人把美洲火鸡当成了经土耳其传入的非洲珍珠鸡。其他语言里火鸡的名字也很有趣，比如“印度鸡”“西方鸡”和“大象鸡”。

lines.en: The U.S. Thanksgiving holiday is symbolized by its traditional food, a large bird we call a turkey. But turkey is certainly not from Turkey.
lines.zh: 美国感恩节的象征是它的传统食物——一种我们叫作 turkey（火鸡）的大鸟。可火鸡当然不是来自 Turkey（土耳其）。

lines.en: In fact, its English name is based on one big mistake. We could say it is a case of mistaken identity.
lines.zh: 事实上，它的英文名字源于一个大错误。可以说这是一场“认错身份”的事件。

lines.en: Let's set the record straight.
lines.zh: 我们来澄清一下。

lines.en: The word "Turkey" has meant "the land of the Turks" since ancient times. The word "turkey" as it refers to the bird first appeared in the English language in the mid-1500s.
lines.zh: 自古以来，Turkey 这个词就指“土耳其人的土地”。而指这种鸟的 turkey 一词，最早出现在 16 世纪中叶的英语里。

lines.en: The misunderstanding over the word happened because of two similar-looking kinds of birds.
lines.zh: 这个词的误会源于两种长得很像的鸟。

lines.en: There is an African bird called the guinea fowl. It has dark feathers with white spots and a patch of brown on the back of its neck. Portuguese traders brought the guinea fowl to Europe through North Africa.
lines.zh: 非洲有一种鸟叫珍珠鸡。它的羽毛是深色的，带着白色斑点，脖子后面有一块褐色。葡萄牙商人经北非把珍珠鸡带到了欧洲。

lines.en: This foreign bird came to Europe through Turkish lands. So, the English thought of the bird as a "Turkish chicken."
lines.zh: 这种外国鸟是经过土耳其人的土地来到欧洲的，所以英国人就把它看作“土耳其鸡”。

lines.en: When Europeans came to North America, they saw a bird that looked like the guinea fowl. This bird was native to the North American continent.
lines.zh: 欧洲人来到北美时，看到一种长得像珍珠鸡的鸟。这种鸟原产于北美大陆。

lines.en: Orin Hargraves is a lexicographer, someone who writes dictionaries. Hargraves explains what happened.
lines.zh: 奥林·哈格雷夫斯是一位词典编纂者，也就是编写词典的人。哈格雷夫斯解释了事情的经过。

lines.en: "Some Europeans saw an American turkey, thought that it was the guinea fowl, which at that time was called the 'turkey cock,' and so gave it the same name."
lines.zh: “一些欧洲人看到了美洲火鸡，以为是珍珠鸡——当时珍珠鸡被叫作‘土耳其公鸡’——于是就给它起了同样的名字。”

lines.en: Hundreds of years later, we continue to call this North American bird "turkey," even though it has no connection at all with the country Turkey, or even with Europe.
lines.zh: 几百年后，我们仍然把这种北美鸟叫作 turkey，尽管它和土耳其这个国家、甚至和欧洲都毫无关系。

lines.en: But English is not the only language with interesting -- and even questionable -- names for this North American bird.
lines.zh: 不过，给这种北美鸟起了有趣——甚至有问题——名字的语言，不只有英语。

lines.en: The Turkish, for their part, call turkey "hindi," the Turkish name for India. The reference to India probably comes from the old, wrong idea that the New World was in Eastern Asia.
lines.zh: 土耳其人管火鸡叫 hindi，这是土耳其语里“印度”的名字。提到印度，可能是来自过去那个错误的观念：以为新大陆在东亚。

lines.en: The French call it "dinde," a name that also connects the bird to India. "D'Inde" means "from India" in the French language. "Turkey" has similar names in several other languages.
lines.zh: 法国人管它叫 dinde，这个名字也把这种鸟和印度联系在一起。D'Inde 在法语里的意思是“来自印度”。还有好几种语言里火鸡的名字也类似。

lines.en: So, what do they call this North American bird in India? Well, in the Hindi language, "turkey" is "tarki."
lines.zh: 那么，在印度人们怎么称呼这种北美鸟呢？嗯，在印地语里，火鸡叫 tarki。

lines.en: But wait, there's more. In Portuguese, the same bird is called "Peru," after the South American nation.
lines.zh: 等等，还没完。在葡萄牙语里，这种鸟叫 Peru，跟南美国家秘鲁同名。

lines.en: Thanks to our VOA Learning English Facebook friends, we have a few more names for "turkey" to share with you.
lines.zh: 感谢 VOA 慢速英语脸书上的朋友们，我们还有几个火鸡的名字要和你分享。

lines.en: The Vietnamese word for the bird is "gà tây" or western chicken. Our Facebook friend Nguyen Duc explains that "local chicken is smaller than western chicken."
lines.zh: 越南语里这种鸟叫 gà tây，意思是“西方鸡”。我们的脸书朋友阮德解释说：“本地鸡比西方鸡小。”

lines.en: A Facebook friend in Myanmar explained that the Burmese word for "turkey" is "kyat sin." The name translates to "elephant chicken" in English.
lines.zh: 一位缅甸的脸书朋友说，缅甸语里“火鸡”叫 kyat sin，翻译成英语是“大象鸡”。

lines.en: "That animal looks like a big chicken," Zaw Myo Win explained.
lines.zh: “那种动物看起来像一只大鸡。”佐·苗·温解释说。

lines.en: The Dari language name for the bird, "fel murgh" also translates to "elephant chicken."
lines.zh: 达利语里这种鸟叫 fel murgh，翻译过来也是“大象鸡”。

lines.en: Abdulla Kawer explained to us that "here in Afghanistan this name represents the size of this delicious meal." He adds that he thinks the descriptive name "elephant chicken" is "better than a country name."
lines.zh: 阿卜杜拉·卡韦尔告诉我们：“在阿富汗，这个名字代表这道美味佳肴的个头。”他还说，他觉得“大象鸡”这个形象的名字“比用国家名好”。

lines.en: I'm Ashley Thompson.
lines.zh: 我是阿什莉·汤普森。

qs.q: Why is the bird called "turkey" in English?
opts: Europeans confused it with a bird that came through Turkey.
qs.a: Europeans confused it with a bird that came through Turkey.
qs.why: "Some Europeans saw an American turkey, thought that it was the guinea fowl."

qs.q: What does the Burmese name "kyat sin" mean?
qs.why: "The name translates to 'elephant chicken' in English."

qs.q: What is turkey called in Portuguese?
qs.why: "In Portuguese, the same bird is called 'Peru.'"

lessons.title: Art, Culture of an Old New York Train Station
lessons.zh: 纽约老地铁站的艺术与文化
lessons.sum: 1904 年开通的纽约市政厅地铁站被誉为“皇冠上的明珠”：拱顶、彩色瓷砖和水晶吊灯。因为站台弯曲太短，容不下长列车，它早已停用，但乘 6 号线坐过终点站，还能看到它的模样。

lines.en: The first subway station in New York City was designed to be a masterpiece and was considered a "jewel in the crown" when it opened.
lines.zh: 纽约市的第一座地铁站被设计成一件杰作，开通时被誉为“皇冠上的明珠”。

lines.en: The trains in New York City's public transportation system, its subway, mostly run underground. Today, the main concern of subway designers is that their systems work correctly.
lines.zh: 纽约市公共交通系统的列车——地铁——大多在地下运行。今天，地铁设计者最关心的是系统能否正常运转。

lines.en: New York's subway opened in 1904. City Hall Station was one of New York City's first underground subway stations. Now called Old City Hall Station, it was built during a time when many public buildings and spaces were designed to appear majestic. The goal was to demonstrate that New York could compete culturally with great European cities, sometimes called metropolises.
lines.zh: 纽约地铁于 1904 年开通。市政厅站是纽约最早的地下地铁站之一。它现在叫“老市政厅站”，建于一个许多公共建筑和场所都被设计得宏伟壮观的时代，目的是显示纽约在文化上可以和欧洲的大城市——有时被称为“大都会”——一较高下。

lines.en: "It was a statement that New York City had arrived at the level of the great European metropolises like London and Paris, Rome, Madrid…that New York City was taking its place as a world city," said Clifton Hood. Hood is a history professor at Hobart and William Smith Colleges in Geneva, New York.
lines.zh: “这是在宣告，纽约市已经达到了伦敦、巴黎、罗马、马德里这些欧洲大都会的水平……纽约正在成为一座世界城市。”克利夫顿·胡德说。胡德是纽约州日内瓦市霍巴特与威廉·史密斯学院的历史学教授。

lines.en: Inside Old City Hall Station, the top is not flat in shape but curved instead. The walls rise up to create a high, round shape known as a vault. Square pieces of glass, called tiles, shine. Some of the lights in the station are called chandeliers. These are beautiful hanging lights that hold many individual light bulbs and look like huge pieces of jewelry.
lines.zh: 在老市政厅站里，顶部不是平的，而是弯的。墙壁向上升起，形成一种叫拱顶的高高的圆形。方形的玻璃片——瓷砖——闪闪发亮。站里有些灯是枝形吊灯，这种漂亮的吊灯上装着许多单独的灯泡，看起来像巨大的珠宝。

lines.en: Polly Desjarlais is with the New York Transit Museum. She said she was "blown away" when she first saw the old station. She used words like "lovely, elegant and really unique space" to describe the station.
lines.zh: 波莉·德斯贾莱斯在纽约交通博物馆工作。她说第一次看到这座老站时，她被“震撼”了。她用“可爱、优雅、非常独特的空间”这样的词来形容它。

lines.en: "I've heard [the station] be described as a celebration of curves, because there are a lot of curves. Everything is sort-of rounded," Desjarlais said.
lines.zh: “我听人把（这座站）形容为一场曲线的庆典，因为曲线特别多，所有东西都是圆圆的。”德斯贾莱斯说。

lines.en: But those beautiful curves are why the station is no longer part of the normal subway system. Its rounded platform cannot fit long trains.
lines.zh: 可正是这些漂亮的曲线，让这座站不再属于正常的地铁系统。它弯曲的站台容不下长列车。

lines.en: "The platform at City Hall is really curved. It's a very, very tight curve, and the platform itself is just over 200 feet long. So, it's short," Desjarlais said. "As the subway got busier…trains got longer, and we added cars…We were growing those platforms and making them longer..."
lines.zh: “市政厅站的站台非常弯，弯得很紧，站台本身只有 200 多英尺长。所以很短，”德斯贾莱斯说，“随着地铁越来越繁忙……列车越来越长，我们加了车厢……我们一直在把站台加长……”

lines.en: Although it is no longer part of the subway system, Old City Hall Station is still being used. One train line, the No. 6, uses the Old City Hall Station to turn around. And while the public cannot enter the station from the street, the members of the New York Transit Museum can see the station a few times a year at a cost of about $50.
lines.zh: 虽然不再属于地铁系统，老市政厅站仍在使用。一条线路——6 号线——用老市政厅站来掉头。公众不能从街上进站，但纽约交通博物馆的会员每年能花约 50 美元参观几次。

lines.en: Over the years, there have been ideas to make the old station a restaurant or a place for travelers to the city to visit. However, security concerns put those ideas to rest. Today, the unofficial way for the public to see the old station is by taking the No. 6 train and staying on after the last stop. Then, the train turns around at the Old City Hall Station, and riders will be able to see the majestic space.
lines.zh: 多年来，有人提议把这座老站改成餐厅或供游客参观的地方，可出于安全考虑，这些想法都被搁置了。如今，公众看这座老站的非官方方法，是坐 6 号线并在终点站后不下车。列车会在老市政厅站掉头，乘客就能看到这个宏伟的空间。

lines.en: I'm Caty Weaver.
lines.zh: 我是凯蒂·韦弗。

qs.q: Why is Old City Hall Station no longer used for passengers?
opts: Its curved platform is too short for long trains.
qs.a: Its curved platform is too short for long trains.
qs.why: "Its rounded platform cannot fit long trains."

qs.q: When did the New York subway open?
qs.why: "New York's subway opened in 1904."

qs.q: How can the public see the old station unofficially?
opts: Stay on the No. 6 train after the last stop.
qs.a: Stay on the No. 6 train after the last stop.
qs.why: "taking the No. 6 train and staying on after the last stop."

gloss: 皇冠上的明珠（最珍贵的部分）

lessons.title: More Americans Interested in 'Bold' Food Tastes
lessons.zh: 越来越多美国人爱上“重口味”
lessons.sum: 研究发现，美国年轻一代吃饭时越来越常选墨西哥菜和亚洲菜，而不是比萨、意面。原因包括社交媒体的影响和拉美裔、亚裔人口的增长。中餐馆遍布每个州，泰国餐馆的数量则远超泰裔人口比例。

lines.en: Researchers who follow trends say more people in the U.S. are interested in "bold" food tastes than ever before.
lines.zh: 研究潮流的人说，对“浓烈”口味感兴趣的美国人比以往任何时候都多。

lines.en: That means an increasing number of Americans enjoy foods from Mexico and Asia while Italian foods like pizza and pasta are not as popular.
lines.zh: 也就是说，越来越多的美国人喜欢墨西哥和亚洲的食物，而比萨、意面这样的意大利食物没那么受欢迎了。

lines.en: Pizza and pasta are still the most popular foods among Americans of all ages. But they have dropped in the opinions of younger people.
lines.zh: 比萨和意面仍然是各年龄段美国人最喜欢的食物，但在年轻人心目中的地位下降了。

lines.en: Mike Kostyo is an analyst at Datassential, a research company in Chicago, Illinois. He works to identify new things that are becoming popular.
lines.zh: 迈克·科斯蒂奥是伊利诺伊州芝加哥一家研究公司 Datassential 的分析师。他的工作是找出正在流行起来的新事物。

lines.en: People who want to go into the restaurant business are his customers. In the past, he said, it was easy to suggest that customers open a restaurant that served Italian food.
lines.zh: 想进入餐饮业的人是他的客户。他说，过去很容易建议客户开一家意大利餐馆。

lines.en: But now, he said, the choice might not be so easy. As a new generation of Americans starts spending money at restaurants, they are choosing Mexican and Asian foods.
lines.zh: 可现在，他说，选择可能就没那么简单了。随着新一代美国人开始在餐馆消费，他们正在选择墨西哥菜和亚洲菜。

lines.en: Datassential's latest food report shows that Americans aged 27 to 42 often choose Mexican food over Italian when they are thinking of going out to eat. Those who are even younger, in Gen Z, like Mexican food the most. Those in Gen Z are younger than 23.
lines.zh: Datassential 最新的饮食报告显示，27 到 42 岁的美国人考虑出去吃饭时，常常选墨西哥菜而不是意大利菜。更年轻的 Z 世代最喜欢墨西哥菜。Z 世代指的是 23 岁以下的人。

lines.en: That means if you visit the U.S., you may start seeing more places to buy foods like tacos than pizza or lasagna.
lines.zh: 这意味着，如果你去美国，可能会开始看到卖塔可之类食物的地方比卖比萨或千层面的地方多。

lines.en: "Before, you know, if you were opening kind of a classic, everybody loves it, restaurant, it would have been a pizza operation. I think in the future, it's going to be a taco operation."
lines.zh: “以前，你知道，如果你要开一家人人都爱的经典餐馆，那会是一家比萨店。我想将来会是一家塔可店。”

lines.en: Kostyo noted that among all Americans, Italian food still holds the top spot. The Baby Boomer generation still likes Italian food. Baby Boomers are between 57 and 75 years old. But Mexican food and Asian food, such as ramen noodles from Japan, are rising fast.
lines.zh: 科斯蒂奥指出，在全体美国人中，意大利菜仍然排第一。婴儿潮一代仍然喜欢意大利菜，他们年龄在 57 到 75 岁之间。但墨西哥菜和亚洲菜——比如日本拉面——正在快速上升。

lines.en: He said many young Americans are influenced by what they see on social media services such as Instagram. People often take photos of their food and share them with friends.
lines.zh: 他说，许多美国年轻人受到他们在 Instagram 等社交媒体上看到的内容的影响。人们经常给食物拍照，分享给朋友。

lines.en: Kostyo recommends that a businessperson who wants to open a restaurant near a college or university should think about a place that serves tacos instead of one that serves pizza.
lines.zh: 科斯蒂奥建议，想在学院或大学附近开餐馆的商人，应该考虑开一家卖塔可的店，而不是卖比萨的。

lines.en: The researchers note that more Americans like the taste of foods from Asia and Latin America than ever before. That is because the number of people in the U.S. from Asia and Latin America is larger than in the past.
lines.zh: 研究人员指出，喜欢亚洲和拉丁美洲食物味道的美国人比以往任何时候都多。这是因为美国来自亚洲和拉丁美洲的人比过去多了。

lines.en: The 2020 Census showed the Latino population grew by 23 percent in only 10 years. Asians make up over 6 percent of the U.S. population.
lines.zh: 2020 年人口普查显示，拉美裔人口仅在 10 年里就增长了 23%。亚裔占美国人口的 6% 以上。

lines.en: Kostyo said many Americans have neighbors or friends from Asia or Latin America. So, they might be introduced to these new foods more often.
lines.zh: 科斯蒂奥说，许多美国人有来自亚洲或拉丁美洲的邻居或朋友，所以他们可能更常接触到这些新食物。

lines.en: The change from Italian food to Mexican food, Kostyo noted, came much faster than he expected. "This is the first time we have ever seen…this change happen in a generation," he said.
lines.zh: 科斯蒂奥指出，从意大利菜到墨西哥菜的转变比他预想的快得多。“这是我们第一次看到……这种转变在一代人之内发生。”他说。

lines.en: Kostyo noted that American tastes are changing. In the past, many Americans were not comfortable with spicy foods. "Every year, their capacity for bold flavors increases, so I think that's also driving some of these changes, as well."
lines.zh: 科斯蒂奥指出，美国人的口味正在变化。过去，许多美国人不太能接受辣的食物。“每年，他们对浓烈味道的承受力都在增加，所以我想这也推动了其中一些变化。”

lines.en: Asian food – from places like China, Japan and Thailand – is known for bold flavors. And a recent report from the Pew Research Center shows Asian food trends.
lines.zh: 来自中国、日本、泰国等地的亚洲菜以味道浓烈出名。皮尤研究中心最近的一份报告揭示了亚洲菜的流行趋势。

lines.en: Sono Shah helped write the Pew report. It said that 71 percent of Asian restaurants in the U.S. serve foods from either China, Japan or Thailand.
lines.zh: 索诺·沙阿参与撰写了皮尤的这份报告。报告说，美国 71% 的亚洲餐馆供应中国、日本或泰国菜。

lines.en: People from those countries make up only 33 percent of the U.S. Asian population.
lines.zh: 而来自这三个国家的人只占美国亚裔人口的 33%。

lines.en: "Chinese restaurants were the most popular, so they're found in every state," Shah said. He added that every state has at least one Japanese or Thai restaurant.
lines.zh: “中餐馆最受欢迎，所以每个州都有，”沙阿说。他还说，每个州至少有一家日本或泰国餐馆。

lines.en: Chinese food, he said, has been in the U.S. for a long time. Japanese restaurants have increased because of the popularity of sushi, an uncooked fish dish. But there are many more Thai restaurants compared to the number of Thai people in the U.S.
lines.zh: 他说，中餐在美国已经有很长时间了。日本餐馆增加，是因为寿司——一种生鱼料理——很受欢迎。但和美国泰国人的数量相比，泰国餐馆多得多。

lines.en: "Eleven percent of all Asian restaurants are Thai. In this piece, we mentioned, you know, the Thai government has sponsored programs abroad to kind of increase the number of Thai restaurants throughout the world as a form of diplomacy."
lines.zh: “所有亚洲餐馆中有 11% 是泰国餐馆。在这篇报告里我们提到，泰国政府在海外资助了一些项目，增加全世界泰国餐馆的数量，作为一种外交方式。”

lines.en: Shah said many people first experience a culture through its food. So, if people like Thai food, they might gain a favorable opinion of Thailand.
lines.zh: 沙阿说，很多人最初是通过食物接触一种文化的。所以，如果人们喜欢泰国菜，就可能对泰国产生好感。

lines.en: While you may find more Asian restaurants in the U.S. than in the past, it is worth noting that they are centered in cities and states where a lot of Asian people live. So about 45 percent of all Asian restaurants are in California, New York, Texas, New Jersey and Washington.
lines.zh: 虽然你可能会发现美国的亚洲餐馆比过去多了，但值得注意的是，它们集中在亚裔居民多的城市和州。所以大约 45% 的亚洲餐馆都在加利福尼亚、纽约、德克萨斯、新泽西和华盛顿州。

lines.en: One final finding about the food interests of Americans? They may fall back on what they see as traditional or "comfort" foods in difficult times. While Kostyo found that young people are interested in trying different foods than their parents, many chose Italian food when asked: "What would they eat if they could only eat one kind of food for the rest of their lives?"
lines.zh: 关于美国人的饮食偏好，最后还有一个发现：在困难时期，他们可能会回归自己心目中的传统食物或“抚慰人心的食物”。科斯蒂奥发现，虽然年轻人有兴趣尝试和父母不同的食物，但被问到“如果余生只能吃一种食物，你会吃什么？”时，很多人选了意大利菜。

lines.en: I'm Dan Friedell. And I'm Jill Robbins
lines.zh: 我是丹·弗里德尔。我是吉尔·罗宾斯。

qs.q: Which food do young Americans (Gen Z) like most?
qs.why: "Those who are even younger, in Gen Z, like Mexican food the most."

qs.q: Why are Asian and Latin American foods more popular?
opts: More people from Asia and Latin America live in the US.
The government asked people to eat them.
qs.a: More people from Asia and Latin America live in the US.
qs.why: "the number of people in the U.S. from Asia and Latin America is larger than in the past."

qs.q: Which Asian restaurants are found in every state?
qs.why: "Chinese restaurants were the most popular, so they're found in every state."

lessons.title: Groundhog Day
lessons.zh: 土拨鼠日：动物界的天气预报
lessons.sum: 每年 2 月 2 日，宾夕法尼亚州小镇庞克瑟托尼的土拨鼠“菲尔”会“预报”春天来得早还是晚。这个传统源自欧洲，各地还有鸭子、鱼、青蛙来“预报”天气。电影《土拨鼠之日》让这个词有了“一再重复”的意思。

lines.en: A groundhog from the small town of Punxsutawney in the state of Pennsylvania again predicted that North America would have six more weeks of winter.
lines.zh: 宾夕法尼亚州小镇庞克瑟托尼的一只土拨鼠，再次预报北美还会有六个星期的冬天。

lines.en: On Thursday, thousands of people gathered around a hill called Gobbler's Knob to watch the yearly event. A group of men in black coats and top hats woke up the groundhog from his long winter sleep. It was as if the groundhog, named Punxsutawney Phil, told them, "I see a shadow…It's six more weeks of winter weather."
lines.zh: 星期四，数千人聚集在一座叫“戈布勒小丘”的山丘周围，观看这项一年一度的活动。一群穿黑外套、戴高顶礼帽的男人把土拨鼠从长长的冬眠中唤醒。仿佛这只名叫“庞克瑟托尼·菲尔”的土拨鼠对他们说：“我看到影子了……还有六个星期的冬天天气。”

lines.en: Since 1887, tradition says that if Punxsutawney Phil does not see his shadow on Groundhog Day, February 2, spring will come early.
lines.zh: 传统上，自 1887 年以来，如果庞克瑟托尼·菲尔在 2 月 2 日土拨鼠日这天没看到自己的影子，春天就会提早来临。

lines.en: Groundhog Day is believed to have come from the ancient European tradition of Candlemas Day. On that day clergy would bless and give out candles to Christians for the long winter.
lines.zh: 人们认为土拨鼠日起源于古代欧洲的圣烛节传统。在那一天，神职人员会祝福蜡烛，分发给基督徒度过漫长的冬天。

lines.en: Some versions of the ancient story say that in parts of Germany, people thought that if a hedgehog saw his shadow on Candlemas Day there would be a "Second Winter" — or six more weeks of bad weather. As Germans migrated to what is now the state of Pennsylvania, they chose another animal, and Groundhog Day was born.
lines.zh: 古老故事的一些版本说，在德国部分地区，人们认为如果刺猬在圣烛节看到自己的影子，就会有“第二个冬天”——也就是再有六个星期的坏天气。德国人迁到今天的宾夕法尼亚州后，选了另一种动物，土拨鼠日就这样诞生了。

lines.en: The tradition is celebrated in many places around the United States and Canada. Countdown to Groundhog Day keeps a list showing 157 such celebrations in North America.
lines.zh: 美国和加拿大很多地方都过这个节。“土拨鼠日倒计时”网站列出了北美 157 个这样的庆祝活动。

lines.en: But the animals do not always agree — and not all of them are groundhogs.
lines.zh: 可是这些动物的预报并不总是一致——而且它们也不全是土拨鼠。

lines.en: Staten Island Chuck, a groundhog once known for biting the finger of then-New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, predicted it would be an early spring. It is hard to argue with that since the National Weather Service said on the social media service Twitter that the lack of snow in the northeast "has been extremely unusual" this year.
lines.zh: 史泰登岛的土拨鼠查克——它曾因咬了时任纽约市长迈克尔·布隆伯格的手指而出名——预报春天会早来。这很难反驳，因为国家气象局在社交媒体推特上说，今年东北部缺少降雪“极不寻常”。

lines.en: In the state of Connecticut, Beardsley Bart, a prairie dog in Bridgeport, also predicted it would be an early spring this year. But Scramble the Duck, Jr. said it would be a long winter in nearby Eastford.
lines.zh: 在康涅狄格州，布里奇波特的一只草原犬鼠比尔兹利·巴特也预报今年春天来得早。可附近伊斯特福德的鸭子“小斯克兰布尔”说冬天会很长。

lines.en: In the state of Ohio, Benny the Bass, a fish, ate a minnow - or a small fish - soon after its release. The Buckeye Lake Region Chamber of Commerce Winterfest said it means there will be an early spring. Tad and Lil, two frogs from Snohomish in the state of Washington, agreed that spring would come early on their own "Groundfrog Day" celebration.
lines.zh: 在俄亥俄州，一条叫“本尼”的鲈鱼被放出后不久就吃了一条小鱼。巴克艾湖地区商会冬季节说，这意味着春天会早来。华盛顿州斯诺霍米什的两只青蛙塔德和莉尔在它们自己的“青蛙日”庆祝活动上，也一致认为春天会早来。

lines.en: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration compared Punxsutawney Phil's forecast in the past 10 years to the actual weather. The agency found that "on average, Phil has gotten it right 40 percent of the time."
lines.zh: 美国国家海洋和大气管理局把庞克瑟托尼·菲尔过去 10 年的预报和实际天气做了比较，发现“平均来说，菲尔有 40% 的时候是对的”。

lines.en: Still, Phil remains the most famous weather predictor thanks to the movie Groundhog Day. In 1993, actor Bill Murray played a weather reporter in the film. The reporter finds himself stuck in time and wakes up on the same day, over and over again, while visiting Punxsutawney.
lines.zh: 不过，多亏了电影《土拨鼠之日》，菲尔仍然是最有名的天气预报“员”。1993 年，演员比尔·默里在片中扮演一名天气预报员。这名预报员在庞克瑟托尼采访时，发现自己被困在时间里，一次又一次地在同一天醒来。

lines.en: The movie popularized the usage of "Groundhog Day" to mean something is happening again and again.
lines.zh: 这部电影让“土拨鼠之日”这个说法流行起来，用来指某件事一再重复发生。

lines.en: I'm Dan Friedell.
lines.zh: 我是丹·弗里德尔。

qs.q: What does it mean if Phil sees his shadow?
qs.why: "I see a shadow…It's six more weeks of winter weather."

qs.q: How often is Phil right, says NOAA?
qs.why: "Phil has gotten it right 40 percent of the time."

qs.q: What does "Groundhog Day" mean in everyday English?
qs.why: "to mean something is happening again and again."

lessons.title: 1-in-5 in US Homes Speaks a Second Language
lessons.zh: 五分之一的美国人在家说第二种语言
lessons.sum: 美国人口普查局说，在家说英语以外语言的人从 1980 年到 2019 年增加了两倍，约 6800 万人。西班牙语最多，其后是汉语、他加禄语、越南语和阿拉伯语。几位移民后代讲述了家里的语言如何影响他们。

lines.en: The U.S. Census Bureau reports that the number of people in the United States who speak a language other than English at home increased by three times between 1980 and 2019.
lines.zh: 美国人口普查局报告说，1980 年到 2019 年间，美国在家说英语以外语言的人数增加了两倍。

lines.en: About one in five people in America speak a second language at home. That is 68 million people.
lines.zh: 美国大约每五个人中就有一个在家说第二种语言，也就是 6800 万人。

lines.en: Dina Arid of California, who is the mother of three children, is one of them. She grew up speaking Arabic at home. She said it is true that the country is "a melting pot," a place where many cultures come together.
lines.zh: 加利福尼亚的迪娜·阿里德是三个孩子的母亲，她就是其中之一。她从小在家说阿拉伯语。她说，美国确实是一个“熔炉”，一个许多文化汇聚的地方。

lines.en: Arabic is one of the five most-spoken second languages in the U.S. Arid speaks mostly English to her children and is trying to teach them a little Arabic.
lines.zh: 阿拉伯语是美国使用最多的五种第二语言之一。阿里德跟孩子们说话主要用英语，同时也在努力教他们一点阿拉伯语。

lines.en: She said some of her cousins "didn't get to learn Arabic." They "always wished that their parents spoke to them in Arabic more so that they have that language," she noted.
lines.zh: 她说，她的一些表亲“没能学会阿拉伯语”。她指出，他们“总希望父母当年多跟他们说阿拉伯语，这样自己就会这门语言了”。

lines.en: Spanish is the most popular second language in the United States. More than 41 million people — about 12 times more than the other most common second languages — speak Spanish at home. Hispanics are the largest minority group in the United States. Fifty-five percent of Spanish speakers were born in the United States.
lines.zh: 西班牙语是美国最流行的第二语言。在家说西班牙语的人超过 4100 万——大约是其他常见第二语言的 12 倍。西班牙裔是美国最大的少数族裔。说西班牙语的人中，55% 出生在美国。

lines.en: The other languages in the top five are Chinese, Tagalog and Vietnamese.
lines.zh: 排在前五的其他语言是汉语、他加禄语和越南语。

lines.en: Jenny Nguyen is studying dentistry in Virginia. Her parents emigrated from Vietnam, so they spoke both English and Vietnamese at home. "I would speak English at school during the day and at night I would only speak Vietnamese just so I could keep the language, Nguyen says. "When I was younger, I didn't understand the importance, but I think now I'm very glad that I'm able to speak and write at such a proficient level."
lines.zh: 珍妮·阮在弗吉尼亚学牙医。她的父母从越南移民过来，所以家里既说英语也说越南语。“白天在学校我说英语，晚上就只说越南语，这样才能保住这门语言，”阮说，“小时候我不明白它的重要性，但现在我很高兴自己能说、能写，而且水平这么高。”

lines.en: She was able to put her language skills to use when she traveled to Vietnam to offer free dental care to poor communities. Many of her co-workers there were also Vietnamese Americans.
lines.zh: 她去越南为贫困社区提供免费牙科治疗时，用上了自己的语言能力。她在那里的很多同事也是越南裔美国人。

lines.en: "They couldn't really communicate with the patients," Nguyen says. "I was one of the very few young volunteers that were able to speak with the patients and communicate with them what was going on."
lines.zh: “他们其实没法和病人交流，”阮说，“我是极少数能和病人说话、告诉他们是怎么回事的年轻志愿者之一。”

lines.en: Cathy Erway is a food writer based in New York City. Erway is using a language application to improve her ability in her mother's native Mandarin Chinese. She said her parents used Chinese between them to talk secretly when their young children were listening
lines.zh: 凯茜·厄韦是纽约市的美食作家。她正在用一款语言应用程序提高自己母亲的母语——普通话——的水平。她说，孩子们小的时候，父母在孩子能听到时用中文说悄悄话。

lines.en: The Census Bureau reports that the number of people who spoke only English at home also increased – by about 25 percent – during the same period.
lines.zh: 人口普查局报告说，同一时期，在家只说英语的人数也增加了约 25%。

lines.en: I'm Jill Robbins.
lines.zh: 我是吉尔·罗宾斯。

qs.q: About how many people in the US speak a second language at home?
qs.why: "That is 68 million people."

qs.q: What is the most popular second language in the US?
qs.why: "Spanish is the most popular second language in the United States."

qs.q: How did Jenny Nguyen use her Vietnamese?
opts: She talked with patients in Vietnam.
qs.a: She talked with patients in Vietnam.
qs.why: "I was one of the very few young volunteers that were able to speak with the patients."

lessons.title: How George Washington Angered Lawmakers over Thanksgiving
lessons.zh: 华盛顿与第一个全国感恩节
lessons.sum: 1789 年，一些国会议员请华盛顿总统宣布全国感恩节，另一些人强烈反对：有人认为这是宗教节日，有人认为这是各州的权力。华盛顿发布了美国第一份总统公告，并请各州州长响应。直到 1941 年，11 月第四个星期四才成为法定假日。

lines.en: In September 1789, the government of the United States was only a few months old. George Washington was president – the nation's first. Congress was new, too. Some of the early lawmakers came to the president with a question: Would he call for a national Thanksgiving?
lines.zh: 1789 年 9 月，美国政府才成立几个月。乔治·华盛顿是总统——这个国家的第一任总统。国会也是新的。一些早期的议员来问总统一个问题：他会不会号召过一个全国性的感恩节？

lines.en: One aim was to help unify the young country, which was made of the 13 former colonies. Calling a national Thanksgiving would be a way to bring Americans together.
lines.zh: 目的之一是帮助团结这个由 13 个前殖民地组成的年轻国家。宣布全国感恩节，是一种把美国人凝聚在一起的方式。

lines.en: But other lawmakers strongly objected to the idea. Critics had two main concerns.
lines.zh: 可另一些议员强烈反对这个主意。批评者主要有两点担心。

lines.en: First, some saw Thanksgiving as a religious holiday. They noted the president could not use the power of the federal government to urge Americans to follow -- or not follow -- a religious tradition.
lines.zh: 第一，有些人把感恩节看作宗教节日。他们指出，总统不能用联邦政府的权力去敦促美国人遵循——或不遵循——某种宗教传统。

lines.en: Second, opponents of the measure believed the president did not have the right to call a national Thanksgiving. That power belonged to the leader of each state, they said.
lines.zh: 第二，反对者认为总统无权宣布全国感恩节。他们说，这项权力属于各州的领导人。

lines.en: In the end, Washington did formally call for a national Thanksgiving. It was the country's first presidential proclamation. In it, he called for a national "day of public thanksgiving and prayer."
lines.zh: 最后，华盛顿还是正式号召过全国感恩节。这是美国的第一份总统公告。在公告中，他号召设立一个全国性的“公共感恩与祈祷日”。

lines.en: He also tried to satisfy opponents of the idea.
lines.zh: 他也尽量让反对者满意。

lines.en: Melanie Kirkpatrick is the writer of "Thanksgiving: The Holiday at the Heart of the American Experience." She explains that Washington sent copies of his proclamation to the leader of each of the 13 states. He asked them to call a national Thanksgiving on the day he had chosen.
lines.zh: 梅兰妮·柯克帕特里克是《感恩节：美国经历核心的节日》一书的作者。她解释说，华盛顿把公告副本寄给了 13 个州的领导人，请他们在他选定的那一天宣布全国感恩节。

lines.en: The president was very well respected, Kirkpatrick notes. And so the state leaders all agreed.
lines.zh: 柯克帕特里克指出，总统非常受人尊敬，所以各州领导人都同意了。

lines.en: In the years that followed, some presidents issued their own proclamations for a day of thanksgiving; many others did not.
lines.zh: 在随后的年份里，一些总统发布了自己的感恩节公告，许多总统则没有。
